category: VSM Studio IDE, compiler toolchains, Visual Designer flowcharts and IoT Builder
description: Firmware development inside Proteus: the Source Code tab (VSM Studio) with its project, build and compiler-configuration commands and the external toolchains it drives per family; Visual Designer's flowchart block set, peripheral gallery, resources, sensor functions, code conversion and hardware programming; and IoT Builder's front-panel editor, control library, MQTT support and the IoT Controller app.

tools.name: New Firmware Project (Source Code tab)
tools.description: Creates the firmware project that lives alongside the schematic in the .pdsprj: you choose the processor family, the controller (which must match the MCU on the schematic), the compiler/toolchain and whether to start from a skeleton main file. The IDE then links the build output to the MCU's Program File automatically, so every successful build is 'programmed' into the simulation without further steps. Existing external projects can be added instead of created.
tools.usage: Source Code tab > Project > New Firmware Project (or the New Project wizard's Firmware page: 'Create Firmware Project') > Family, Controller, Compiler > OK; Project > Add Existing Project for external code

parameters.name: Family / Controller
parameters.description: e.g. PIC16 / PIC16F877A - filters the compiler list.

parameters.name: Compiler
parameters.description: Installed toolchain detected by Compilers Configuration.

parameters.name: Create Quick Start Files
parameters.description: Generates main.c with the family's header includes.

tools.example: Project > New Firmware Project > AVR / ATmega328P / AVR-GCC > edit main.c > Build Project > Play: the ELF is attached to the ATmega328P on the schematic.
tools.notes: Only one firmware project per processor; multi-MCU designs add one project per controller. Visual Designer projects are a flowchart flavour of the same mechanism.

tools.name: Build > Build Project
tools.description: Compiles and links the firmware project with the configured toolchain, writing compiler output to the pane at the bottom of the IDE; on success the debug file (COF/ELF/OMF/...) is attached to the MCU model and the simulation can be run immediately. Errors are listed with file/line and clicking one navigates to the offending source line. Rebuild forces a full recompile and Clean removes the build products.
tools.usage: Source Code tab > Build > Build Project (or the Build toolbar icon); Build > Rebuild Project / Clean Project as needed
tools.example: Missing semicolon: Build reports 'main.c:42: syntax error'; click the line, fix, Build again, then press Play.
tools.notes: Linker errors are not navigable - fix include paths/libraries in Build > Project Settings. VSM Studio adds the debug switches (e.g. -g) automatically.

tools.name: Build > Project Settings
tools.description: Per-project compiler and linker options: optimisation level, additional include and library paths, defines, extra compiler/linker flags, the output/debug file name, and for Arduino/Visual Designer projects the programming settings (interface, COM port, port speed, programmer, resource uploader). VSM Studio pre-populates the settings needed for simulation debugging so only project-specific additions are normally required.
tools.usage: Source Code tab > Build > Project Settings > tabs for compiler / linker / programming > OK

parameters.name: Optimisation
parameters.description: -O0 recommended while debugging so stepping matches source lines.

parameters.name: Include / library paths
parameters.description: Extra directories for headers and libraries.

parameters.name: Programmer / Port / Port Speed
parameters.description: Hardware upload settings (Arduino: AVRDUDE, COMx, 115200; Yun: YUNSSH).

tools.example: Add C:\libs\fatfs to the include path and fatfs.a to the linker to build an SD-card project.
tools.notes: Optimised builds can make variables 'optimized out' in the Variables window.

tools.name: Compilers Configuration (System / Config menu)
tools.description: The dialogue listing every toolchain VSM Studio supports with its installed/configured status. 'Check All' rescans the PC for installations and configures those found; open-source compilers (AVR-GCC, GCC for ARM, SDCC, the Arduino core, XC8 free edition where allowed) can be downloaded and installed from Labcenter's servers with the Download button, while proprietary ones have a 'goto website' link. It runs automatically on first use of the Source Code tab.
tools.usage: Source Code tab > System (Proteus 8) or Config (Proteus 9) menu > Compilers Configuration > Check All / Download / Goto Website / Manual path

parameters.name: Check All
parameters.description: Rescan and auto-configure installed compilers.

parameters.name: Download
parameters.description: Fetch and install a free toolchain from Labcenter.

parameters.name: Manual
parameters.description: Point at a non-standard install directory.

tools.example: Install Hi-Tech PICC 9.8 from Microchip's site, return to the dialogue and press Check All - the row turns 'installed' and the F1 evaluation demo builds.
tools.notes: Results of the scan are echoed in the output window. A compiler installed after Proteus needs Check All before it appears in New Firmware Project.

tools.name: Source editor (breakpoints, disassembly, bookmarks, find)
tools.description: The VSM Studio code editor: syntax colouring for C/assembly/Python, breakpoints toggled by clicking left of the line number (or double-click/context menu), 'Clear all breakpoints', a Disassembly view toggled from the context menu for instruction-level stepping, bookmarks, find/replace across files, go-to-line and code folding. When the simulation pauses, the current line is highlighted and the Variables and Watch windows dock below.
tools.usage: Source Code tab > open file from the project tree > click the gutter to set a breakpoint; right-click > Disassembly / Clear all breakpoints

parameters.name: Breakpoint
parameters.description: Line breakpoint; shown as a red marker in the gutter.

parameters.name: Disassembly
parameters.description: Toggle between C and generated assembly for the same location.

tools.example: Set a breakpoint on the button-release branch of main(); Play; press the button in the active popup; the IDE halts on that line with PORTB visible in the Variables window.
tools.notes: Breakpoints are stored in the project. Python (MicroPython) sources support the same breakpoint/step model.

tools.name: Variables window and Output window
tools.description: Docked panes at the bottom of the IDE: the Variables window lists globals and the locals of the current scope with values that refresh on every pause/step (right-click > Add to Watch Window to track one live; hover shows values in the editor), and the Output window shows compiler/linker output, compiler-check results and programmer (upload) messages with clickable error lines.
tools.usage: Source Code tab > Debug menu (VSM Studio) > Variables; Output pane below the editor

parameters.name: Display format
parameters.description: Hex/decimal/binary per variable via context menu.

tools.example: Pause at the LED-off block: both 'lux' and 'distance' appear in Variables with the values read from the Grove sensors.
tools.notes: Only the Watch Window updates during free-running simulation; Variables refreshes when paused.

tools.name: Program physical hardware (Upload / Programmer settings)
tools.description: After simulation, the same firmware is transferred to the real board from the IDE: Arduino targets via AVRDUDE over USB (interface = board type, COM port from Device Manager, port speed from the board's datasheet, e.g. 115200 for the Uno, 57600 for the Yun), the Yun also over Wi-Fi/Ethernet with the YUNSSH programmer, and Raspberry Pi over SSH (hostname/IP, username, password) with the Visual Designer runtime and resources copied automatically. The resource uploader also writes bitmaps/WAV files to the SD card.
tools.usage: Source Code / Visual Designer tab > Project Settings > Programmer, Interface, Port, Port Speed > Upload/Program icon

parameters.name: Interface
parameters.description: Arduino board type (Uno, Mega...) or SSH target.

parameters.name: Port / Port Speed
parameters.description: COMx and baud (115200 Uno, 57600 Yun).

parameters.name: Resource Uploader
parameters.description: Helper used to transfer Visual Designer resources to the card.

tools.example: Plug in the Uno, Device Manager shows 'USB Serial Device (COM7)': set Port COM7, 115200, press Upload - AVRDUDE output appears in the Output window.
tools.notes: A 'variant mismatch' error means the selected board differs from the one the project was built for; the real clock may also differ from the simulation clock (set 'Clock For Delays').

tools.name: Embed Files option (.pdsprj firmware container)
tools.description: Project option that stores all source and debug files inside the .pdsprj container instead of a sibling folder, so a single file carries schematic, PCB, firmware and build output. It keeps student and archive projects self-contained and avoids broken Program File paths when a project is moved between machines.
tools.usage: Firmware project settings > tick 'Embed Files'
tools.example: Tick Embed Files before emailing a lab exercise; the recipient opens the .pdsprj and can Build and Play immediately.
tools.notes: Very large projects (big resource files) make the .pdsprj correspondingly large; disable embedding for shared version-controlled source trees.

tools.name: Microchip MPLAB XC8 (PIC10/12/16/18 toolchain)
tools.description: Microchip's C compiler for 8-bit PIC, one of the toolchains VSM Studio detects and configures; it produces the COF debug file Proteus loads for source-level debugging. The free edition can be installed from within Compilers Configuration and the Getting Started firmware tutorials use it (or its Hi-Tech PICC predecessor).
tools.usage: Compilers Configuration > 'Microchip XC8' row > Download or Goto Website; New Firmware Project > Family PIC16/PIC18 > Compiler XC8

parameters.name: Debug output
parameters.description: COF file (set automatically in debug configuration).

tools.example: #include <xc.h>; #pragma config settings; VSM Studio passes the chip selection and -g equivalent flags; Build then Play.
tools.notes: Configuration bits are taken from the firmware image, so #pragma config must be correct for the oscillator mode used. Older MPLAB C18 and Hi-Tech PICC (PIC10/12/16, PIC18, dsPIC) remain supported for legacy code.

tools.name: Microchip MPLAB XC16 (PIC24 / dsPIC33 toolchain)
tools.description: The 16-bit Microchip compiler used for PIC24 and dsPIC33 firmware projects; VSM Studio configures it to emit COF/ELF debug output and the processor models load either. Its predecessor MPLAB C30 is also on the supported list for older projects.
tools.usage: New Firmware Project > Family PIC24 or dsPIC33 > Compiler XC16

parameters.name: Debug output
parameters.description: COF or ELF with DWARF.

tools.example: dsPIC33FJ32MC204 motor-control project built with XC16 -O0 so the PWM ISR can be stepped line by line.
tools.notes: MPLAB XC32 is not listed because PIC32 is not simulated.

tools.name: MPASM / MPLAB C18 / MPLAB C30 / CCS C (legacy Microchip toolchains)
tools.description: Additional Microchip-family toolchains VSM Studio recognises: MPASM (assembler for all 8-bit PIC, COF output), MPLAB C18 (PIC18 C), MPLAB C30 (PIC24/dsPIC C) and the third-party CCS C compiler for PIC. They allow existing assembly and pre-XC projects to be built and debugged inside Proteus without conversion.
tools.usage: Compilers Configuration > check the row is installed > New Firmware Project > pick the compiler
tools.example: Assemble a PIC16F84A .asm tutorial with MPASM and single-step the instructions with the W register in the CPU Registers window.
tools.notes: MPASM ships inside MPLAB X (pic-as replaced it in newer XC8); point Compilers Configuration at the installed copy if auto-detect misses it.

tools.name: WinAVR / AVR-GCC and AVRASM (AVR toolchains)
tools.description: The GNU C toolchain for AVR (WinAVR distribution or a stand-alone avr-gcc) downloadable from Labcenter's servers, producing ELF/DWARF files for the AVR models, and Atmel's AVRASM assembler (assembler-only projects). VSM Studio sets -mmcu and -g from the controller selection.
tools.usage: Compilers Configuration > 'WinAVR' Download; New Firmware Project > Family AVR > Compiler WinAVR (GCC) or AVRASM

parameters.name: -mmcu
parameters.description: Set from the chosen controller.

parameters.name: F_CPU
parameters.description: Define it to match the Processor Clock Frequency property.

tools.example: ATmega16 LCD project: #define F_CPU 8000000UL, build with WinAVR, run with Clock Frequency 8MHz.
tools.notes: Also used under the hood for Arduino sketches (the Arduino AVR core wraps avr-gcc).

tools.name: Arduino AVR core (sketch toolchain)
tools.description: The Arduino build environment (core libraries + avr-gcc) that VSM Studio downloads and drives for Arduino-family projects and Visual Designer for Arduino: sketches (.ino) with setup()/loop() are compiled with the board's variant files and the resulting ELF is attached to the Arduino board model. Standard Arduino libraries (Wire, SPI, SD, Servo, LiquidCrystal, Adafruit_*) build unchanged, and the Visual Designer peripherals expose their methods as calls into these libraries.
tools.usage: New Firmware Project > Family Arduino > Controller Arduino Uno > Compiler 'Arduino AVR'; write the sketch in the editor; Build

parameters.name: Board variant
parameters.description: Selected by the controller (Uno, Mega, Leonardo, Nano, Yun).

tools.example: Serial.begin(9600); Serial.println("hi") - build, run, and the text appears on a Virtual Terminal wired to TX/RX.
tools.notes: The STM32 Arduino core (Blue Pill) is configured the same way for the STM32F103C8T6 target. Convert a Visual Designer flowchart to a sketch to hand-edit it.

tools.name: BASCOM AVR and Proton BASIC (BASIC compilers)
tools.description: BASIC-language toolchains on the supported list: BASCOM AVR (produces an OBJ debug file the AVR models load) and Proton BASIC for PIC (BAS format). They let BASIC-based teaching material be simulated with source-level stepping in Proteus.
tools.usage: Compilers Configuration > BASCOM AVR / Proton; New Firmware Project > Compiler BASCOM AVR
tools.example: BASCOM 'Config Lcd' program on an ATmega8 with an LM016L; step the Lcd statements and watch the glass update.
tools.notes: Both are commercial compilers installed separately; VSM Studio only configures paths and debug options.

tools.name: SDCC and ASEM-51 (8051 toolchains)
tools.description: Free 8051 toolchains: SDCC (Small Device C Compiler, downloadable from Labcenter, producing CDB debug data) and the ASEM-51 assembler (assembler-only projects). VSM Studio adds the memory-model and debug options and links the output to the 8051 model.
tools.usage: Compilers Configuration > SDCC Download; New Firmware Project > Family 8051 > Compiler SDCC or ASEM-51

parameters.name: --debug
parameters.description: Emits the CDB file used for source stepping (set by VSM Studio).

tools.example: AT89C52 traffic-light program in SDCC; break inside the timer ISR and inspect TH0/TL0 in the CPU registers window.
tools.notes: Keil C51 (OMF51) and IAR (UBROF) are the commercial alternatives on the same list.

tools.name: Keil uVision (C51 for 8051, MDK for ARM)
tools.description: Keil's commercial toolchains are supported both as VSM Studio compilers (Keil uVision4 C51 for 8051 with OMF51 output; Keil for ARM/MDK producing ELF/DWARF for Cortex-M and ARM7) and as remote-debug hosts, where uVision drives the Proteus simulation through Labcenter's Keil debugger driver.
tools.usage: Compilers Configuration > Keil rows; or in uVision: Options for Target > Debug > 'Proteus VSM Simulator' driver with Use Remote Debug Monitor enabled in Proteus

parameters.name: Debug file
parameters.description: OMF51 (.omf/.abs) for C51, ELF/AXF for MDK.

tools.example: STM32F103 MDK project: build in uVision, start a debug session with the Proteus driver, and step HAL code while the LCD animates in Proteus.
tools.notes: Ensure the Program File on the schematic points to the same image uVision built.

tools.name: GCC for ARM and IAR Embedded Workbench (ARM toolchains)
tools.description: The GNU Arm Embedded toolchain (downloadable from Labcenter and used for LPC2000, Cortex-M0/M3/M4 projects, ELF/DWARF output) and IAR Embedded Workbench for ARM (UBROF/ELF, with an IAR debugger driver for remote debugging). CubeMX/STM32Cube HAL projects can be imported into a GCC firmware project or debugged from STM32CubeIDE via GDB in Proteus 9.2.
tools.usage: Compilers Configuration > 'GCC for ARM' Download / 'IAR for ARM'; New Firmware Project > Family ARM Cortex-M3 > Compiler GCC for ARM

parameters.name: Linker script / startup
parameters.description: Provided by the family template; adjust for custom memory maps.

tools.example: LPC1114 GPIO blink built with GCC for ARM; break in SysTick_Handler and read the NVIC state in the CPU registers window.
tools.notes: IAR is also on the 8051 list (UBROF). Debugger drivers for IAR and Keil UV3 are noted in the ARM7 specification.

tools.name: Code Composer Studio and GCC for MSP430 (TI toolchains)
tools.description: TI's Code Composer (for MSP430 and for Piccolo/C2000) producing COFF/DWARF debug files, and the open-source GCC for MSP430 downloadable from Labcenter, are the toolchains VSM Studio configures for the Texas Instruments families.
tools.usage: Compilers Configuration > 'Code Composer for MSP430' / 'Code Composer for PICCOLO' / 'GCC for MSP430'; New Firmware Project > Family MSP430 or PICCOLO
tools.example: MSP430G2553 low-power timer demo built with GCC for MSP430; single-step __bis_SR_register(LPM3_bits) and watch simulation time jump to the next interrupt.
tools.notes: Code Composer projects can also be built in CCS and their .out attached directly as the Program File.

tools.name: Visual Designer project tree (Peripherals, Resources, Flowchart sheets)
tools.description: The left-hand tree of a Visual Designer project with three roles: it lists the CPU and every added peripheral with their drag-and-drop methods (the primary way hardware is driven), holds resource files (bitmaps, WAV, text) for the storage model, and organises flowchart sheets (Main plus any subroutine sheets added for large programs). Right-click menus add peripherals, resources, IoT controls and sheets, rename items and open their settings.
tools.usage: Visual Designer tab > Project Tree > right-click > Add Peripheral / Add Resource / Add Sheet / Add IoT control; expand a peripheral and drag a method onto the flowchart
tools.example: Expand 'Grove LED' > drag 'on' into the Loop routine; double-click 'Main' to switch sheets.
tools.notes: Dragging the peripheral itself (not a method) places its sensor function as a decision block.

tools.name: Event / Subroutine Start Block
tools.description: The block that begins a routine: paired with an End Block it defines a subroutine (only a name is needed, which then appears in Subroutine Call dialogues) or an event handler, where a trigger is also specified - a timer match/periodic trigger, an external interrupt pin, a serial event or an IoT control action such as a button press. A new Arduino project starts with two event/end pairs, Setup and Loop.
tools.usage: Drag the Event block icon onto the sheet > edit: Name; for handlers choose Trigger (e.g. Timer1 match, periodic interval, pin interrupt, IoT button)

parameters.name: Name
parameters.description: Routine name used by Subroutine Call blocks.

parameters.name: Trigger
parameters.description: Optional event source; the periodic trigger consumes a CPU timer.

tools.example: Event 'onButton' triggered by the IoT push button: drag from the button in the project tree onto the sheet to create it in one step.
tools.notes: A periodic trigger uses one of the CPU timers - do not reuse that timer elsewhere (e.g. a servo shield).

tools.name: End Block
tools.description: Terminates a routine or event handler started by an Event block; execution returns to the caller (or the scheduler for handlers). Every routine needs one, and the Setup/Loop pair generated for a new project must keep their End blocks for the flowchart to compile.
tools.usage: Drag the End block icon under the last statement of the routine and connect the flowline
tools.example: Single-stepping to the END block of Loop shows the LED state just before the loop repeats.
tools.notes: If Setup/Loop were deleted, add an Event block named Setup or Loop plus an End block to restore them.

tools.name: Assignment Block
tools.description: Assigns a value or expression to a variable and is also where variables are created, edited and deleted (name, type - integer/float/string/boolean/array - and initial value). Expressions may reference other variables, peripheral read methods and arithmetic/logical operators.
tools.usage: Drag the Assignment icon > edit: pick or create a variable > enter the expression (e.g. speed = 200, count = count + 1)

parameters.name: Variable
parameters.description: Target variable (new or existing).

parameters.name: Expression
parameters.description: Value to assign.

tools.example: In Setup: speed = 150; in Loop: motor.setSpeed(speed) via the peripheral method.
tools.notes: Variables appear in the Variables window when the simulation is paused.

tools.name: Decision Block
tools.description: A boolean test with YES and NO exits that branches program flow; the dialogue takes any boolean expression (comparisons on variables or sensor readings, logical AND/OR). The YES/NO labels can be swapped from the context menu to suit the layout, and dropping a peripheral (not a method) onto the sheet creates a decision on its sensor function automatically.
tools.usage: Drag the Decision icon > edit: expression (e.g. lux < 100) > wire YES and NO exits; right-click > Swap YES/NO

parameters.name: Expression
parameters.description: Boolean test; sensor functions return TRUE/FALSE.

tools.example: Nightlight: Decision 'readLuminance() < 100' then a second Decision 'readDistance() < 20' on the YES path, then LED on.
tools.notes: Both exits must be connected; an unconnected NO path is a compile error.

tools.name: Loop Construct Block (Count, For-Next, While-Wend, Repeat-Until)
tools.description: A paired block that wraps a section of flowchart in a loop configured from a dialogue: Count loop (execute N times), For-Next (start, stop, step with a loop variable), While-Wend (test at the top; body may run zero times) and Repeat-Until (test at the bottom; body runs at least once). Logic blocks are placed between the loop's start and end markers.
tools.usage: Drag the Loop icon (places start and end markers) > edit: Loop type and parameters > drop blocks inside

parameters.name: Loop type
parameters.description: Count / For-Next / While-Wend / Repeat-Until.

parameters.name: Count or Start/Stop/Step or Condition
parameters.description: Depending on type.

tools.example: For i = 0 to 7 step 1: shiftOut bit i to the 74HC595 breakout; Next.
tools.notes: A Delay inside a tight loop stalls other processing on Arduino, as in the delay() function.

tools.name: Subroutine Call Block
tools.description: Calls a routine defined elsewhere on the flowchart by an Event/End pair; the dialogue's combo box lists every named routine. It keeps Loop readable by moving display updates, motor stop sequences and similar work into their own sheets or areas.
tools.usage: Drag the Subroutine Call icon > edit: choose the routine name > OK

parameters.name: Routine
parameters.description: Name of an existing Event block.

tools.example: Loop calls 'stopMotors' after a run; Step Into (F11) follows execution into the subroutine and back.
tools.notes: Create the subroutine first, otherwise the combo box is empty.

tools.name: Time Delay Block
tools.description: Inserts a blocking delay of a specified duration (ms/us) in the program, equivalent to Arduino delay(); during the delay no sensor reading or pin manipulation occurs, though interrupts and event handlers still run. Use it for blink timing and debouncing; for periodic work prefer an Event with a periodic trigger.
tools.usage: Drag the Time Delay icon > edit: delay value and units

parameters.name: Delay
parameters.description: Duration (e.g. 100ms).

tools.example: LED on > Delay 500ms > LED off > Delay 500ms inside Loop.
tools.notes: Simulation time advances by the delay when stepped over, so the schematic shows the elapsed effects immediately.

tools.name: I/O (Peripheral) Operation Block
tools.description: Performs an action on hardware - a CPU method (digitalWrite, analogRead, pinMode, timers, serial) or a method of an added peripheral (LCD print, motor run, sensor read, TFT drawBitmap). It is created by dragging a method from the project tree, and its dialogue exposes the method's arguments (pins, values, variables to receive results).
tools.usage: Project Tree > expand CPU or a peripheral > drag the method onto the flowchart > edit arguments

parameters.name: Arguments
parameters.description: Method parameters; may be literals or variables.

parameters.name: Result variable
parameters.description: For read methods, the variable that receives the value.

tools.example: Drag 'readLuminance()' from the Grove luminance sensor into Loop and store the result in 'lux'.
tools.notes: With no peripherals added, only CPU methods are available. Methods map to the Arduino/Python library calls seen after 'Convert to source'.

tools.name: Stored Data Block
tools.description: Specifies an action on a storage object (the SD card of a shield or breakout): open/create a file, read, write/append, close, and directory operations on the filestore, typically used with resource files such as text logs. Shields that include their own resource methods (TFT drawBitmap, Wave shield play) should be driven by dragging the resource itself rather than this block.
tools.usage: Project Tree > right-click > Add Resource (file) > drag onto the sheet or use the Storage block icon > choose the filestore method

parameters.name: Method
parameters.description: open / read / write / close etc. on the filestore.

parameters.name: Filename
parameters.description: 8.3 filename for FAT16 compatibility.

tools.example: Data-logger: open 'LOG.TXT' for append in Setup; in Loop write the temperature string and close.
tools.notes: Requires an SD card in an included shield or an SD breakout; check the card image size in the shield settings before programming hardware.

tools.name: Interconnector Block
tools.description: Pairs of numbered 'virtual wire' blocks that join flowchart columns without a drawn flowline, so long sequences can be split into separate columns on the sheet. Placed as a pair and numbered to match, or created by right-clicking a flowline and choosing split; two interconnects dragged over each other rejoin the line.
tools.usage: Drag two Interconnector icons, link them into the flow and give both the same number; or right-click a flowline > Split

parameters.name: Number
parameters.description: Matching pairs share the same number.

tools.example: Break the 40-block Loop into two columns with interconnector 1 at the bottom of column one and the top of column two.
tools.notes: Purely a layout aid; it generates no code.

tools.name: Comment Block and Edit Notes (block tooltips)
tools.description: Two ways to document a flowchart: the Comment block is a free-format text block that is always visible on the sheet, and Edit Notes on any block's context menu attaches a tooltip comment (marked by a small blue triangle) shown on hover. Neither affects the generated code.
tools.usage: Drag the Comment icon > type text; or right-click any block > Edit Notes
tools.example: Comment 'Sensor sockets: proximity A0, luminance A2 - see Grove wiring' beside Setup.
tools.notes: Comments are exported to the generated sketch/Python as source comments.

tools.name: Peripheral Gallery (Add Peripheral: Arduino shields, Grove, breakout boards, Pi HATs)
tools.description: The browser opened by Add Peripheral, organised by category: Arduino shields (Arduino Motor Shield R3 variants, Adafruit motor/servo/relay/TFT/NeoPixel/Wave/data-logger shields, Yun shield), Grove modules (Starter Kit LEDs, buttons, buzzer, relay, OLED, 4-digit and RGB LCD displays, temperature/light/proximity/ultrasonic/sound sensors, servo), breakout boards (SD card SPI, DHT11/DHT22, ADC/DAC modules, servo, GPS, keypads, Nokia 3310 LCD, 74HC595 ...), Raspberry Pi HATs (Adafruit, Pimoroni, GrovePi+) and Internet-of-Things items (ESP8266, Yun shield). Picking an item auto-places its circuitry on the schematic, connects it by terminal name and adds its methods to the project tree.
tools.usage: Visual Designer > Project Tree > right-click > Add Peripheral > category (Arduino Shields / Grove / Breakout / Adafruit / Pimoroni / Internet of Things) > double-click the item

parameters.name: Connector / header
parameters.description: Grove socket or pin assignment; change it on the schematic part if two modules clash (e.g. A0 vs A2).

tools.example: Add Grove 80cm IR proximity (socket A0) and Grove luminance (socket A2): the proximity module uses analogue pin A1, so A1 must be left free.
tools.notes: Check shield compatibility: some share a CPU timer or pins, and the Uno may run out of RAM with several large shields.

tools.name: Sensor functions (peripheral TRUE/FALSE decisions)
tools.description: Every peripheral exposes a 'sensor function' that returns TRUE or FALSE for its basic state - a button returns TRUE while pressed, an LED TRUE while on, a proximity sensor TRUE when an object is within range. Dropping the peripheral node itself onto the flowchart inserts the sensor function as a Decision block, which is the idiomatic way to react to inputs without separate read/compare blocks.
tools.usage: Drag the peripheral (not a method) from the Project Tree onto the sheet > a Decision block on its sensor function appears > wire YES/NO
tools.example: Drop 'Grove Button' into Loop: YES > LED on; NO > LED off.
tools.notes: Inputs like buttons have no methods in the tree - the sensor function is their only interface.

tools.name: Resources and the filestore (SD card image, bitmaps, WAV files)
tools.description: Visual Designer's storage model: resource files (pictures, audio clips, text) added to the project tree are written into the SD card image of an included shield/breakout when the simulation starts (and to the real card when programming), and dragging a resource onto the flowchart inserts the method that consumes it (drawBitmap() on a TFT shield, play() on a Wave shield). Filenames follow 8.3 for FAT16 and the image size must be set large enough in the shield's settings.
tools.usage: Project Tree > Resources > right-click > Add Resource > choose file; set SD card image size on the shield; drag the resource into the flowchart

parameters.name: Image size
parameters.description: Capacity of the simulated card; WAV files need more than bitmaps.

parameters.name: 8.3 filename
parameters.description: Name stem <= 8 characters for FAT16.

tools.example: Add LOGO.BMP, drag it into Loop (drawBitmap() is inserted), Build, Play: the TFT shows the image streamed from the card image.
tools.notes: Programming real hardware requires a FAT16/FAT32 card in the shield; the Resource Uploader copies the files.

tools.name: Convert flowchart to source (Arduino sketch / Python script / MicroPython)
tools.description: Generates a text-source project from a flowchart - an Arduino sketch for AVR/STM32 targets, a Python program for Raspberry Pi, MicroPython for Pico/ESP32 - so the program can be extended by hand with the same peripheral libraries and still be simulated and debugged. The conversion is one-way: after converting, development continues in the Source Code tab.
tools.usage: Visual Designer > Project menu > Convert to Source (Arduino sketch / Python) > confirm
tools.example: Prototype a Grove data logger as a flowchart, convert to a sketch, then add a custom CRC routine in C.
tools.notes: Keep a copy of the .pdsprj before converting if you may want to return to the flowchart.

tools.name: Robot Turtle simulation (Visual Designer)
tools.description: An animated two-wheeled turtle robot target (Arduino-based, introduced in Proteus 8.6 and extended in 9.1) with line sensors (CNY70-style), bumpers/proximity sensors and motors, driven on a virtual arena from flowchart methods (forward, turn, read line). Proteus 9.1 added multi-colour tracks and collect-and-deposit challenges, making it the educational robotics track of Visual Designer.
tools.usage: New Project > Visual Designer for Arduino > Robot Turtle target; add the arena/track resources; program with the turtle's methods

parameters.name: Track / challenge
parameters.description: Arena layout with coloured lines and pick-up items (9.1).

tools.example: Line-follower: Loop reads left/right line sensors and calls turn methods; watch the turtle track the loop on the arena view.
tools.notes: Listed as 'Robot Turtles' in the Visual Designer product line; requires the Arduino Visual Designer licence.

tools.name: MicroPython REPL console (Visual Designer for MicroPython)
tools.description: An interactive MicroPython prompt attached to the running simulation of a Pico/ESP32/Pyboard target: commands can be issued while the project runs, variables inspected or modified in real time and hardware poked (machine.Pin(...).value(1)) without editing the flowchart or script. Driver blocks for attached hardware appear automatically in the project tree.
tools.usage: MicroPython project > Play > open the REPL console pane > type expressions at the >>> prompt
tools.example: While the temperature loop runs, type 'threshold = 30' in the REPL and watch the fan relay behaviour change immediately.
tools.notes: Available with Proteus VSM for MicroPython; pausing the simulation freezes the REPL too.

tools.name: IoT Control Panel editor (front panel design)
tools.description: IoT Builder's drag-and-drop editor for the remote user interface: controls from the IoT controls library are placed on a panel sized for the target phone/tablet (Panel Settings), styled with selectable themes (basic, retro, steampunk, modern, classic ...), and arranged with geometry properties, alignment and 'element replication' for button groups; text and graphic primitives, background images (JPG/SVG/PNG) and multiple tabs (New Tab on 'Main Controls') complete the panel. Each placed control adds methods and events to the project tree for binding to the flowchart or code.
tools.usage: Visual Designer > Project Tree > right-click the target (Yun/Pi/Pico) > Add IoT control; double-click 'IoT Control Panel' to open the editor; right-click Main Controls > Panel Settings / New Tab

parameters.name: Panel size
parameters.description: Match the target device resolution (see mydevice.io comparison).

parameters.name: Theme
parameters.description: Visual style applied to all controls.

parameters.name: Element replication
parameters.description: Count and spacing for button groups/radio sets.

tools.example: Logging thermometer panel: mercury thermometer (Display Controls), time-axis line chart (Chart Controls) and a radio-button group minute/hour/day plus a Reset push button.
tools.notes: Advanced panel graphics can be edited in Inkscape (SVG) per the 'Advanced Panel Design' chapter.

tools.name: IoT controls library (Buttons, Switches, Displays, Indicators, Dials and Sliders, Alerts, Text boxes/Terminals, Clocks/Timers, Line/Bar charts, Histogram, Wind Rose)
tools.description: The control set of IoT Builder, each with design-time properties and programming methods/events: Buttons (push, toggle, radio groups; AutoLamp property makes a button self-indicating), Switches, Displays (numeric/text displays, thermometer, gauges), Indicators (lamps), Dials and Sliders (knobs and sliders returning values), Alerts (pop-up messages), Text input, Teletype terminal and Text log controls, Clocks and Timers, Line chart (time x-axis, setTimeRange()), Bar chart, Histogram and the Wind Rose control. Values flow to firmware as events and from firmware via set methods (setTemperature(), setLamp(), setValue()).
tools.usage: IoT Control Panel > Add IoT control > category > control; then in the flowchart drag the control's methods (e.g. setLamp) or events (button pressed) from the project tree

parameters.name: AutoLamp
parameters.description: Button property: lamp follows the button state automatically (toggle behaviour).

parameters.name: Design-time configuration
parameters.description: Range, labels, colours, replication per control.

tools.example: thermometer.setTemperature(tempC) in Loop; lineChart.addPoint(tempC); reset button event calls lineChart.clear().
tools.notes: Front-panel actions are processed in the event handlers of the flowchart; a control that is not placed on the panel (e.g. a timer) can still be used from code.

tools.name: IoT Controller app and web front end
tools.description: Free iOS/Android 'Proteus IoT Controller' app (and any browser) that hosts the designed front panel: it discovers IoT Builder simulations on the same Wi-Fi network - and later the real Yun/Pi/MicroPython hardware - and renders the panel with live control, so the appliance is driven from a phone during simulation and after deployment. A message in Proteus's panel indicates when a remote controller has taken over the display.
tools.usage: Install the Proteus IoT Controller app > phone on the same network as the PC > Play the simulation > app: Discover > select the panel by name (Panel Settings sets the name)

parameters.name: Panel name
parameters.description: Identifier shown in the app's discovery list.

tools.example: Press the on-screen button in the app: the LED turns on in the simulation and the panel's lamp indicator lights.
tools.notes: Stopping from the app does not stop the simulation - press Stop in Proteus. Deployment then serves the same panel from the hardware's web server.

tools.name: MQTT support (IoT Builder publish/subscribe)
tools.description: Built-in MQTT client methods for IoT Builder targets (enhanced in Proteus 8.11): firmware can publish sensor data to topics and subscribe to command topics on a broker, enabling multi-device systems - e.g. an Arduino appliance and a Raspberry Pi control unit - to exchange messages both in simulation and on deployed hardware. Methods appear in the project tree like any peripheral method.
tools.usage: Project Tree > IoT target > MQTT methods (connect(broker), publish(topic, value), subscribe(topic)) > drag into the flowchart; subscription events create handlers

parameters.name: Broker address / port
parameters.description: MQTT server on the network.

parameters.name: Topic
parameters.description: Publish/subscribe channel name.

tools.example: Pico W publishes 'home/temp' every 10s; a Pi 3 project subscribes and updates a gauge on its own panel.
tools.notes: Requires the IoT Builder module; the simulated device uses the host PC's network to reach the broker.

tools.name: IoT Builder targets (Arduino Yun / Yun shield / ESP8266, Raspberry Pi 3, MicroPython boards)
tools.description: Which hardware can host an IoT Builder front panel: the Arduino Yun board, the Yun shield mounted on an Uno/Mega, an Uno with an ESP8266 breakout ('UNO+ESP8266'), the Raspberry Pi 3 (Visual Designer for Raspberry Pi) and, from Proteus 9.1, MicroPython boards - Pico W, ESP32-S3, Nano ESP32. The panel and web server are deployed to the networked part of the target while the flowchart/C/Python firmware runs on the MCU.
tools.usage: New flowchart project > target selection; for shields/breakouts add them from the Internet of Things peripheral category
tools.example: Classroom: simulate with the Yun, deploy to an Uno + Yun shield over YUNSSH; students control it from the IoT Controller app.
tools.notes: Programming methods per target are described in the 'Programming the Hardware' chapter (Pi 3, Yun via SSH, Yun via USB).
